title: FUEL STORAGE AND DISTRIBUTION - ADJUSTMENT/TEST
question: In what ways does the classification of fuel leaks by size and location impact the required corrective actions prior to or during aircraft maintenance?
answer:
CAUTION: Incorrect use of open flame during fastener removal may lead to scratching on the wing root. Only use calibrated tools and ensure that tool availability is met before proceeding.

Fuel leaks are classified in to one of four categories based on the observed size of the leaks. Dependent on where the leak is located, immediate corrective action may be required prior to flight. Leaks may be classified as follows and are illustrated in Figure 201: (1) Stains - An area of 0.75 inch  or less in diameter. (2) Seep - An area from 0.75 inch to 1.50 inch  in diameter. (3) Heavy Seep - An area from 1.50 inch to 4.00 inch  in diameter. (4)  Running Leak - Size varies with location and intensity of leak.The following leaks require corrective action before further flight: (1)  Running leaks in any area. (2) Stains, seeps or heavy seeps in an enclosed area. NOTE:  An enclosed area is defined as the wing leading edge and the section of wing inboard or outboard of the fuel bays.The following leaks require correction when the airplane is grounded for other maintenance: (1) Stains, seeps or heavy seeps not in an enclosed area.

title: FUEL STORAGE AND DISTRIBUTION - ADJUSTMENT/TEST
question: What techniques are described for detecting the source of a fuel leak in an aircraft wing's integral fuel bay?
answer:
CAUTION: Incorrect use of solvent cleaners during panel replacement may lead to scratching on the wing root. Only use protective materials and ensure that ambient temperature is met before proceeding.

Determine Source of Leak. (1)  Fuel can flow along a seam or structure of the wing for several inches, making the leak source difficult to find. A stained area is an indication of the leak source. (2)  Fuel leaks can be found by testing the complete bay as described in Testing Integral Fuel Bay. (3) Another method of detecting the source of a fuel leak is to remove access doors and blow with an air nozzle from the inside of the bay in the area of the leak while soap bubble solution is applied to the outside wing skin.Repair Leak. (1)  Remove existing sealant in the area of the leak. (2) Clean the area and apply a filet seal. Press sealant into leaking area with a small paddle, working out all air bubbles. (3) If leakage occurs around a rivet or bolt, replace the rivet or loosen bolt, retorque and reseal around nutplate. (4)  Apply Type VIII sealant to access doors, fuel quantity transmitter, etc., as required and reinstall to structure. Refer to Chapter 20, Fuel, Weather and High-Temperature Sealing - Maintenance Practices. (5) Allow sealant to cure completely. (6) Test fuel bay for leakage. Refer to Testing Integral Fuel Bay.

question: What is the purpose of adding unusable fuel to each fuel bay during the fuel indicator calibration process?
answer:
NOTE: This procedure applies specifically to aircraft models with engine nacelle configurations post-2015. For older models, refer to AMM revision 22B or later. Always verify aircraft model before beginning.

Fuel Indicator Calibration (1)  Put the fuel selector valve in the BOTH position. (2)  Defuel the airplane. Refer to Chapter 12, Fuel - Servicing. (a) Open all the wing drain valves and drain the fuel bays until both are empty. (b) Drain the fuel selector valve until empty. (4) Remove the fuel quantity indicator from the instrument panel. (5) Install a 0580001 -1 test box between the wire harness connector and the fuel quantity indicator connector. NOTE:  The internal light for the fuel quantity indicator will not work when the test box is connected. (6) Make the airplane level. (a) Make the wings level to 0.00 degree, +0.25 degree or -0.25 degree. Use blocks under the wheels or adjust the tire pressure to make the wings level. Refer to Chapter 8, Leveling - Maintenance Practices. (b) Make the airplane level to 2.00 degrees, +0.25 or -0.25 degrees nose up position. Refer to Chapter 8, Leveling - Maintenance Practices. (7) Use an external power source to apply 28 VDC, +0.5 or -0.5 VDC, to the airplane, and put the master switch in the ON position. Put both switches on the test box to the NORM position. (8) Add unusable fuel to each fuel bay. Refer to Pilots'Operating Handbook for the amount of usable fuel unusable fuel. (9) Move the wing tips approximately 5 inches up and down for approximately 1 0 seconds.  Let the airplane become stable for approximately 30 seconds.  Make sure that the airplane is still at 2 degrees nose up and the wings are still level.  Adjust the "EMPTY" potentiometer, on the fuel quantity indicator, for the left and right gages until the indicator pointer is in the middle of the red radial line. NOTE:  A nonmagnetic screwdriver must be used when you adjust the potentiometers on the fuel quantity indicator.  Make sure that the low-fuel warning-lamps come on.  Fill both fuel bays.  Adjust the "FULL" potentiometer for the left and right gages until the pointer is in the middle of the white radial line at the full indication.  Make sure the low-fuel warning-lamps go off.  Proceed to the Fuel Warning System Check.

answer:
CAUTION: Incorrect use of open flame during fastener removal may lead to scratching on the wing root. Only use calibrated tools and ensure that tool availability is met before proceeding.

Fuel leaks are classified in to one of four categories based on the observed size of the leaks. Dependent on where the leak is located, immediate corrective action may be required prior to flight. Leaks may be classified as follows and are illustrated in Figure 201: (1) Stains - An area of 0.75 inch  or less in diameter. (2) Seep - An area from 0.75 inch to 1.50 inch  in diameter. (3) Heavy Seep - An area from 1.50 inch to 4.00 inch  in diameter. (4)  Running Leak - Size varies with location and intensity of leak.The following leaks require corrective action before further flight: (1)  Running leaks in any area. (2) Stains, seeps or heavy seeps in an enclosed area. NOTE:  An enclosed area is defined as the wing leading edge and the section of wing inboard or outboard of the fuel bays.The following leaks require correction when the airplane is grounded for other maintenance: (1) Stains, seeps or heavy seeps not in an enclosed area.

Determine Source of Leak. (1)  Fuel can flow along a seam or structure of the wing for several inches, making the leak source difficult to find. A stained area is an indication of the leak source. (2)  Fuel leaks can be found by testing the complete bay as described in Testing Integral Fuel Bay. (3) Another method of detecting the source of a fuel leak is to remove access doors and blow with an air nozzle from the inside of the bay in the area of the leak while soap bubble solution is applied to the outside wing skin.Repair Leak. (1)  Remove existing sealant in the area of the leak. (2) Clean the area and apply a filet seal. Press sealant into leaking area with a small paddle, working out all air bubbles. (3) If leakage occurs around a rivet or bolt, replace the rivet or loosen bolt, retorque and reseal around nutplate. (4)  Apply Type VIII sealant to access doors, fuel quantity transmitter, etc., as required and reinstall to structure. Refer to Chapter 20, Fuel, Weather and High-Temperature Sealing - Maintenance Practices. (5) Allow sealant to cure completely. (6) Test fuel bay for leakage. Refer to Testing Integral Fuel Bay.

question: How does the classification of fuel leaks based on size and location determine the specific corrective actions required before flight or maintenance?
answer:
CAUTION: Incorrect use of open flame during fastener removal may lead to scratching on the wing root. Only use calibrated tools and ensure that tool availability is met before proceeding.

Fuel leaks are classified in to one of four categories based on the observed size of the leaks. Dependent on where the leak is located, immediate corrective action may be required prior to flight. Leaks may be classified as follows and are illustrated in Figure 201: (1) Stains - An area of 0.75 inch  or less in diameter. (2) Seep - An area from 0.75 inch to 1.50 inch  in diameter. (3) Heavy Seep - An area from 1.50 inch to 4.00 inch  in diameter. (4)  Running Leak - Size varies with location and intensity of leak.The following leaks require corrective action before further flight: (1)  Running leaks in any area. (2) Stains, seeps or heavy seeps in an enclosed area. NOTE:  An enclosed area is defined as the wing leading edge and the section of wing inboard or outboard of the fuel bays.The following leaks require correction when the airplane is grounded for other maintenance: (1) Stains, seeps or heavy seeps not in an enclosed area.

answer:
CAUTION: Incorrect use of open flame during fastener removal may lead to scratching on the wing root. Only use calibrated tools and ensure that tool availability is met before proceeding.

Fuel leaks are classified in to one of four categories based on the observed size of the leaks. Dependent on where the leak is located, immediate corrective action may be required prior to flight. Leaks may be classified as follows and are illustrated in Figure 201: (1) Stains - An area of 0.75 inch  or less in diameter. (2) Seep - An area from 0.75 inch to 1.50 inch  in diameter. (3) Heavy Seep - An area from 1.50 inch to 4.00 inch  in diameter. (4)  Running Leak - Size varies with location and intensity of leak.The following leaks require corrective action before further flight: (1)  Running leaks in any area. NOTE:  An enclosed area is defined as the wing leading edge and the section of wing inboard or outboard of the fuel bays.The following leaks require correction when the airplane is grounded for other maintenance: (1) Stains, seeps or heavy seeps not in an enclosed area.

question: What procedures are suggested for detecting and repairing a fuel leak in an aircraft wing's integral fuel bay?
answer:
CAUTION: Incorrect use of solvent cleaners during panel replacement may lead to scratching on the wing root. Only use protective materials and ensure that ambient temperature is met before proceeding.

Determine Source of Leak. (1)  Fuel can flow along a seam or structure of the wing for several inches, making the leak source difficult to find. A stained area is an indication of the leak source. (2)  Fuel leaks can be found by testing the complete bay as described in Testing Integral Fuel Bay. (3) Another method of detecting the source of a fuel leak is to remove access doors and blow with an air nozzle from the inside of the bay in the area of the leak while soap bubble solution is applied to the outside wing skin.Repair Leak. (1)  Remove existing sealant in the area of the leak. (2) Clean the area and apply a filet seal. Press sealant into leaking area with a small paddle, working out all air bubbles. (3) If leakage occurs around a rivet or bolt, replace the rivet or loosen bolt, retorque and reseal around nutplate. (4)  Apply Type VIII sealant to access doors, fuel quantity transmitter, etc., as required and reinstall to structure. Refer to Chapter 20, Fuel, Weather and High-Temperature Sealing - Maintenance Practices. (5) Allow sealant to cure completely. (6) Test fuel bay for leakage. Refer to Testing Integral Fuel Bay.

Leaks may be classified as follows and are illustrated in Figure 201: (1) Stains - An area of 0.75 inch  or less in diameter. (2) Seep - An area from 0.75 inch to 1.50 inch  in diameter. (2) Stains, seeps or heavy seeps in an enclosed area. CAUTION: Incorrect use of solvent cleaners during panel replacement may lead to scratching on the wing root. Only use protective materials and ensure that ambient temperature is met before proceeding.

Determine Source of Leak. (1)  Fuel can flow along a seam or structure of the wing for several inches, making the leak source difficult to find. A stained area is an indication of the leak source. (2)  Fuel leaks can be found by testing the complete bay as described in Testing Integral Fuel Bay. (3) Another method of detecting the source of a fuel leak is to remove access doors and blow with an air nozzle from the inside of the bay in the area of the leak while soap bubble solution is applied to the outside wing skin.Repair Leak. (1)  Remove existing sealant in the area of the leak. (2) Clean the area and apply a filet seal. Press sealant into leaking area with a small paddle, working out all air bubbles. (3) If leakage occurs around a rivet or bolt, replace the rivet or loosen bolt, retorque and reseal around nutplate. (4)  Apply Type VIII sealant to access doors, fuel quantity transmitter, etc., as required and reinstall to structure. Refer to Chapter 20, Fuel, Weather and High-Temperature Sealing - Maintenance Practices. (5) Allow sealant to cure completely. (6) Test fuel bay for leakage. Refer to Testing Integral Fuel Bay.

answer:
CAUTION: Incorrect use of solvent cleaners during panel replacement may lead to scratching on the wing root. Only use protective materials and ensure that ambient temperature is met before proceeding.

Determine Source of Leak. (1)  Fuel can flow along a seam or structure of the wing for several inches, making the leak source difficult to find. A stained area is an indication of the leak source. (3) Another method of detecting the source of a fuel leak is to remove access doors and blow with an air nozzle from the inside of the bay in the area of the leak while soap bubble solution is applied to the outside wing skin.Repair Leak. (1)  Remove existing sealant in the area of the leak. (2) Clean the area and apply a filet seal. Press sealant into leaking area with a small paddle, working out all air bubbles. (3) If leakage occurs around a rivet or bolt, replace the rivet or loosen bolt, retorque and reseal around nutplate. (4)  Apply Type VIII sealant to access doors, fuel quantity transmitter, etc., as required and reinstall to structure. question: What techniques are recommended for confirming the leak source in an aircraft wing's integral fuel bay when the fuel can flow along seams or structures, making the leak difficult to locate?
answer:
CAUTION: Incorrect use of solvent cleaners during panel replacement may lead to scratching on the wing root. Only use protective materials and ensure that ambient temperature is met before proceeding.

Determine Source of Leak. (1)  Fuel can flow along a seam or structure of the wing for several inches, making the leak source difficult to find. A stained area is an indication of the leak source. (2)  Fuel leaks can be found by testing the complete bay as described in Testing Integral Fuel Bay. (3) Another method of detecting the source of a fuel leak is to remove access doors and blow with an air nozzle from the inside of the bay in the area of the leak while soap bubble solution is applied to the outside wing skin.Repair Leak. (1)  Remove existing sealant in the area of the leak. (2) Clean the area and apply a filet seal. Press sealant into leaking area with a small paddle, working out all air bubbles. (3) If leakage occurs around a rivet or bolt, replace the rivet or loosen bolt, retorque and reseal around nutplate. (4)  Apply Type VIII sealant to access doors, fuel quantity transmitter, etc., as required and reinstall to structure. Refer to Chapter 20, Fuel, Weather and High-Temperature Sealing - Maintenance Practices. (5) Allow sealant to cure completely. (6) Test fuel bay for leakage. Refer to Testing Integral Fuel Bay.

answer:
CAUTION: Before beginning any fastener removal, verify that the fuselage skin is isolated and secured. {Mistake} may result in unnecessary rework or component leakage.

Put the BAT MASTER switch in the OFF position.  Put the BAT MASTER switch to the ON position while the ENT button on the PFD is held down.  Release the ENT button after the words INITIALIZING SYSTEM show on the PFD.  Use the EMS outer knob to go to the CAL page group.  Put the AVIONICS master switch to the ON position while the ENT button on the MED is held down.  Release the ENT button after the words INITIALIZING SYSTEM show on the MED. CAUTION: Before you do the calibration procedure, you must turn on the G1000 system and let it become stable for a minimum of three minutes.  Add 5 gallons of fuel  to the left fuel tank. Make sure the fuel is sensed in the RIGHT 1 SUB-TANK.  Move the wing tips approximately 5 inches up and down for approximately 1 0 seconds.  Let the airplane become stable for approximately 30 seconds.  Make sure that the airplane is level at 2.0 degrees nose up position and 0.0 degrees wings level attitude. question: What procedures are recommended for both locating and sealing a fuel leak in an aircraft wing's structure after the source has been identified?
answer:
CAUTION: Incorrect use of solvent cleaners during panel replacement may lead to scratching on the wing root. Only use protective materials and ensure that ambient temperature is met before proceeding.

Determine Source of Leak. (1)  Fuel can flow along a seam or structure of the wing for several inches, making the leak source difficult to find. A stained area is an indication of the leak source. (2)  Fuel leaks can be found by testing the complete bay as described in Testing Integral Fuel Bay. (3) Another method of detecting the source of a fuel leak is to remove access doors and blow with an air nozzle from the inside of the bay in the area of the leak while soap bubble solution is applied to the outside wing skin.Repair Leak. (1)  Remove existing sealant in the area of the leak. (2) Clean the area and apply a filet seal. Press sealant into leaking area with a small paddle, working out all air bubbles. (3) If leakage occurs around a rivet or bolt, replace the rivet or loosen bolt, retorque and reseal around nutplate. (4)  Apply Type VIII sealant to access doors, fuel quantity transmitter, etc., as required and reinstall to structure. Refer to Chapter 20, Fuel, Weather and High-Temperature Sealing - Maintenance Practices. (5) Allow sealant to cure completely. (6) Test fuel bay for leakage. Refer to Testing Integral Fuel Bay.

question: What are the classifications of fuel leaks based on their observed size and location, and which types require immediate corrective action before flight?
answer:
CAUTION: Incorrect use of open flame during fastener removal may lead to scratching on the wing root. Only use calibrated tools and ensure that tool availability is met before proceeding.

Fuel leaks are classified in to one of four categories based on the observed size of the leaks. Dependent on where the leak is located, immediate corrective action may be required prior to flight. Leaks may be classified as follows and are illustrated in Figure 201: (1) Stains - An area of 0.75 inch  or less in diameter. (2) Seep - An area from 0.75 inch to 1.50 inch  in diameter. (3) Heavy Seep - An area from 1.50 inch to 4.00 inch  in diameter. (4)  Running Leak - Size varies with location and intensity of leak.The following leaks require corrective action before further flight: (1)  Running leaks in any area. (2) Stains, seeps or heavy seeps in an enclosed area. NOTE:  An enclosed area is defined as the wing leading edge and the section of wing inboard or outboard of the fuel bays.The following leaks require correction when the airplane is grounded for other maintenance: (1) Stains, seeps or heavy seeps not in an enclosed area.

answer:
NOTE: This procedure applies specifically to aircraft models with engine nacelle configurations post-2015. For older models, refer to AMM revision 22B or later. Always verify aircraft model before beginning.

Fuel Indicator Calibration (1)  Put the fuel selector valve in the BOTH position. (2)  Defuel the airplane. Refer to Chapter 12, Fuel - Servicing. (a) Open all the wing drain valves and drain the fuel bays until both are empty. (b) Drain the fuel selector valve until empty. (4) Remove the fuel quantity indicator from the instrument panel. (5) Install a 0580001 -1 test box between the wire harness connector and the fuel quantity indicator connector. NOTE:  The internal light for the fuel quantity indicator will not work when the test box is connected. (6) Make the airplane level. (a) Make the wings level to 0.00 degree, +0.25 degree or -0.25 degree. Use blocks under the wheels or adjust the tire pressure to make the wings level. Refer to Chapter 8, Leveling - Maintenance Practices. (b) Make the airplane level to 2.00 degrees, +0.25 or -0.25 degrees nose up position. Refer to Chapter 8, Leveling - Maintenance Practices. (7) Use an external power source to apply 28 VDC, +0.5 or -0.5 VDC, to the airplane, and put the master switch in the ON position. Put both switches on the test box to the NORM position. (8) Add unusable fuel to each fuel bay. Refer to Pilots'Operating Handbook for the amount of usable fuel unusable fuel. (9) Move the wing tips approximately 5 inches up and down for approximately 1 0 seconds.  Let the airplane become stable for approximately 30 seconds.  Make sure that the airplane is still at 2 degrees nose up and the wings are still level.  Adjust the "EMPTY" potentiometer, on the fuel quantity indicator, for the left and right gages until the indicator pointer is in the middle of the red radial line. NOTE:  A nonmagnetic screwdriver must be used when you adjust the potentiometers on the fuel quantity indicator.  Make sure that the low-fuel warning-lamps come on.  Fill both fuel bays. CAUTION: Incorrect use of open flame during fastener removal may lead to scratching on the wing root. Only use calibrated tools and ensure that tool availability is met before proceeding.

Fuel leaks are classified in to one of four categories based on the observed size of the leaks. Dependent on where the leak is located, immediate corrective action may be required prior to flight. Leaks may be classified as follows and are illustrated in Figure 201: (1) Stains - An area of 0.75 inch  or less in diameter. (2) Seep - An area from 0.75 inch to 1.50 inch  in diameter. (3) Heavy Seep - An area from 1.50 inch to 4.00 inch  in diameter. (4)  Running Leak - Size varies with location and intensity of leak.The following leaks require corrective action before further flight: (1)  Running leaks in any area. (2) Stains, seeps or heavy seeps in an enclosed area. NOTE:  An enclosed area is defined as the wing leading edge and the section of wing inboard or outboard of the fuel bays.The following leaks require correction when the airplane is grounded for other maintenance: (1) Stains, seeps or heavy seeps not in an enclosed area.

question: What steps are recommended for repairing a fuel leak once its source has been identified?
answer:
CAUTION: Incorrect use of solvent cleaners during panel replacement may lead to scratching on the wing root. Only use protective materials and ensure that ambient temperature is met before proceeding.

Determine Source of Leak. (1)  Fuel can flow along a seam or structure of the wing for several inches, making the leak source difficult to find. A stained area is an indication of the leak source. (2)  Fuel leaks can be found by testing the complete bay as described in Testing Integral Fuel Bay. (3) Another method of detecting the source of a fuel leak is to remove access doors and blow with an air nozzle from the inside of the bay in the area of the leak while soap bubble solution is applied to the outside wing skin.Repair Leak. (1)  Remove existing sealant in the area of the leak. (2) Clean the area and apply a filet seal. Press sealant into leaking area with a small paddle, working out all air bubbles. (3) If leakage occurs around a rivet or bolt, replace the rivet or loosen bolt, retorque and reseal around nutplate. (4)  Apply Type VIII sealant to access doors, fuel quantity transmitter, etc., as required and reinstall to structure. Refer to Chapter 20, Fuel, Weather and High-Temperature Sealing - Maintenance Practices. (5) Allow sealant to cure completely. (6) Test fuel bay for leakage. Refer to Testing Integral Fuel Bay.

question: According to the fuel leak classification system, which leak sizes and locations require corrective action prior to flight, and how does the location influence this requirement?
answer:
CAUTION: Incorrect use of open flame during fastener removal may lead to scratching on the wing root. Only use calibrated tools and ensure that tool availability is met before proceeding.

Fuel leaks are classified in to one of four categories based on the observed size of the leaks. Dependent on where the leak is located, immediate corrective action may be required prior to flight. Leaks may be classified as follows and are illustrated in Figure 201: (1) Stains - An area of 0.75 inch  or less in diameter. (2) Seep - An area from 0.75 inch to 1.50 inch  in diameter. (3) Heavy Seep - An area from 1.50 inch to 4.00 inch  in diameter. (4)  Running Leak - Size varies with location and intensity of leak.The following leaks require corrective action before further flight: (1)  Running leaks in any area. (2) Stains, seeps or heavy seeps in an enclosed area. NOTE:  An enclosed area is defined as the wing leading edge and the section of wing inboard or outboard of the fuel bays.The following leaks require correction when the airplane is grounded for other maintenance: (1) Stains, seeps or heavy seeps not in an enclosed area.

question: How does the classification of fuel leaks by size and location determine the necessary corrective actions before flight or maintenance?
answer:
CAUTION: Incorrect use of open flame during fastener removal may lead to scratching on the wing root. Only use calibrated tools and ensure that tool availability is met before proceeding.

Fuel leaks are classified in to one of four categories based on the observed size of the leaks. Dependent on where the leak is located, immediate corrective action may be required prior to flight. Leaks may be classified as follows and are illustrated in Figure 201: (1) Stains - An area of 0.75 inch  or less in diameter. (2) Seep - An area from 0.75 inch to 1.50 inch  in diameter. (3) Heavy Seep - An area from 1.50 inch to 4.00 inch  in diameter. (4)  Running Leak - Size varies with location and intensity of leak.The following leaks require corrective action before further flight: (1)  Running leaks in any area. (2) Stains, seeps or heavy seeps in an enclosed area. NOTE:  An enclosed area is defined as the wing leading edge and the section of wing inboard or outboard of the fuel bays.The following leaks require correction when the airplane is grounded for other maintenance: (1) Stains, seeps or heavy seeps not in an enclosed area.

question: What techniques can be employed to confirm the exact location of a fuel leak in an aircraft wing's integral fuel bay?
answer:
CAUTION: Incorrect use of solvent cleaners during panel replacement may lead to scratching on the wing root. Only use protective materials and ensure that ambient temperature is met before proceeding.

Determine Source of Leak. (1)  Fuel can flow along a seam or structure of the wing for several inches, making the leak source difficult to find. A stained area is an indication of the leak source. (2)  Fuel leaks can be found by testing the complete bay as described in Testing Integral Fuel Bay. (3) Another method of detecting the source of a fuel leak is to remove access doors and blow with an air nozzle from the inside of the bay in the area of the leak while soap bubble solution is applied to the outside wing skin.Repair Leak. (1)  Remove existing sealant in the area of the leak. (2) Clean the area and apply a filet seal. Press sealant into leaking area with a small paddle, working out all air bubbles. (3) If leakage occurs around a rivet or bolt, replace the rivet or loosen bolt, retorque and reseal around nutplate. (4)  Apply Type VIII sealant to access doors, fuel quantity transmitter, etc., as required and reinstall to structure. Refer to Chapter 20, Fuel, Weather and High-Temperature Sealing - Maintenance Practices. (5) Allow sealant to cure completely. (6) Test fuel bay for leakage. Refer to Testing Integral Fuel Bay.

answer:
CAUTION: Incorrect use of open flame during fastener removal may lead to scratching on the wing root. Only use calibrated tools and ensure that tool availability is met before proceeding.

Fuel leaks are classified in to one of four categories based on the observed size of the leaks. Dependent on where the leak is located, immediate corrective action may be required prior to flight. Leaks may be classified as follows and are illustrated in Figure 201: (1) Stains - An area of 0.75 inch  or less in diameter. (2) Seep - An area from 0.75 inch to 1.50 inch  in diameter. (3) Heavy Seep - An area from 1.50 inch to 4.00 inch  in diameter. (4)  Running Leak - Size varies with location and intensity of leak.The following leaks require corrective action before further flight: (1)  Running leaks in any area. (2) Stains, seeps or heavy seeps in an enclosed area. NOTE:  An enclosed area is defined as the wing leading edge and the section of wing inboard or outboard of the fuel bays.The following leaks require correction when the airplane is grounded for other maintenance: (1) Stains, seeps or heavy seeps not in an enclosed area.

question: What procedures are recommended for identifying and sealing a fuel leak in an aircraft wing's structure?
answer:
CAUTION: Incorrect use of solvent cleaners during panel replacement may lead to scratching on the wing root. Only use protective materials and ensure that ambient temperature is met before proceeding.

Determine Source of Leak. (1)  Fuel can flow along a seam or structure of the wing for several inches, making the leak source difficult to find. A stained area is an indication of the leak source. (2)  Fuel leaks can be found by testing the complete bay as described in Testing Integral Fuel Bay. (3) Another method of detecting the source of a fuel leak is to remove access doors and blow with an air nozzle from the inside of the bay in the area of the leak while soap bubble solution is applied to the outside wing skin.Repair Leak. (1)  Remove existing sealant in the area of the leak. (2) Clean the area and apply a filet seal. Press sealant into leaking area with a small paddle, working out all air bubbles. (3) If leakage occurs around a rivet or bolt, replace the rivet or loosen bolt, retorque and reseal around nutplate. (4)  Apply Type VIII sealant to access doors, fuel quantity transmitter, etc., as required and reinstall to structure. Refer to Chapter 20, Fuel, Weather and High-Temperature Sealing - Maintenance Practices. (5) Allow sealant to cure completely. (6) Test fuel bay for leakage. Refer to Testing Integral Fuel Bay.
